utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the delay. Good afternoon, everybody. I'm sorry about the delay. It's just matters beyond my control that kept me away. May the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case IT-06-90-PT, the Prosecutor v. Ante Gotovina, Ivan Cermak and Mladen Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And let me welcome everybody to this session of the court. May we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Alan Tieger and Marks Moore with the OTP with case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Greg Kehoe and Luka Misetic for General Gotovina, along with case manager Ana Katalinic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Cedo Prodanovic and Jadranka Slokovic for General Cermak. Your Honour, Goran Mikulicic, to my left, David Gold, legal assistant, and Mr. Vlada Randunic, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just confirm that the parties who are on videolink can hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours [Inaudible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can hear somebody talking, but I don't hear anything here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Can you hear me now? Good afternoon. Can you hear me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you talk again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Ram Doraiswamy from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ram Doraiswamy, but I can't hear you very well. I don't know whether other members in court do hear him. Can we just talk again? Let's see if we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] ... Court Officer in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still don't hear anything. I see Mr. Misetic is shaking his head. He's not hearing, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The same over there. What shall we do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that technical people are coming just now. Shall we give them a few minutes? I don't know how long they will be. Could you please try again? Let's see if we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can hear you now. I don't know whether everybody else can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Ram Doraiswamy from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good, I can hear you. Can you just give us time and let everybody else switch on to the right button. Can everybody hear him now? Okay, thank you very much. That being sorted out, may we just find out the condition of the accused? Mr. Gotovina, will you please stand up? Do you have anything to say about your health, your state of health? THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for asking me. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, thank you for asking me. I am fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are fine. Thank you very much. And before you sit down, let me just find out if you can hear me in a language that you understand. I should have asked you that before I asked you about your health. THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you have any comments about your conditions of detention? THE ACCUSED GOTOVINA: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. I do know that Mr. Markac and Mr. Cermak are out on provisional release, but nevertheless I don't think there's anything wrong in finding out about their health conditions, too. Can they hear me in a language they understand? Can I be heard? THE ACCUSED CERMAK: [Interpretation] I can hear you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cermak. And Mr. Markac, can you hear me? THE ACCUSED MARKAC: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I start with you, Mr. Cermak. Do you have anything to tell us about your state of health? THE ACCUSED CERMAK: [Interpretation] Well, I can say that I don't feel very well, as a matter of fact, I feel very bad. It was the decision of the Trial Chamber to leave my without my Defence team that I've been cooperating with for the past nine years. At any rate, I am duty-bound to abide by the decision of the Trial Chamber and find new lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you on that one, Mr. Cermak? The question related to your state of health and not to your representation in court. Do you have anything to -- THE ACCUSED CERMAK: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- say about your state of health? Did I get an answer to that? THE ACCUSED CERMAK: [Interpretation] I don't feel well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In health, sir, or in emotions? THE ACCUSED CERMAK: [Interpretation] As regards my emotions and the state that I'm in right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry about that, and let's hope that your emotions will resolve in time. Mr. Markac, anything about your health? THE ACCUSED MARKAC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, you know that my health has been impaired. However, my medical team together with me is taking all measures to keep the state of my health at the given level and to improve it, if at all possible. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Markac. We're sorry that your health is not that good, but we are also happy to hear that your doctors are doing something good about it. Thank you so much. Can we deal with the question of the last status conference? The last status conference in this case was held on the 3rd of April, 2007. Pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a status conference shall be convened within 120 days of the last in order to organise exchanges between the parties to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial and to allow the accused to raise issues in relation to their case. I believe this morning a 65 ter meeting was held in preparation for this conference. Let me just say, then, that the issues that are on the agenda deal with, first of all, the conflict of interest matters. I'll start with Mr. Separovic's conflict of interest. The Trial Chamber's decision on conflict of 27th of February, 2007, and the subsequent decision on finding of misconduct of 6th of March, 2007, were upheld by the Appeals Chamber on the 4th of May, 2007. Mr. Markac has been aware of this conflict of interest issue for over four months now. I would like to hear from Mr. Markac what progress he has made on finding another counsel to replace Mr. Separovic and when he expects new counsel to take over this case. Mr. Mikulicic, are you able to answer that question on behalf of Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very gladly, Your Honour. The Defence of General Markac is taking all steps in order to find another colleague who would, together with me, represent our client, Mr. Markac. We are negotiating with a few candidates. However, regrettably these negotiations have not really advanced. The reason is that every one of the attorneys we have contacted puts two questions, and I have no answer to those questions; namely, when the trial will start and for how long it will go on. Those questions are understandable because any colleague who would take over the Defence of General Markac would have to organise himself or herself in his domicile law office, and he cannot do that without knowing these basic parameters. However, in spite of that, we seem to be on the right track, and it seems possible for us to retain yet another person for the Markac Defence. It would be very helpful if we could get answers to those two questions from the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the first question is a chicken-and-egg question. You want to know when the trial will start. The Chamber wants to know when counsel will be available and ready to start the case, to be able to schedule the case. So I'm not quite sure which must come first. Must we first get counsel on board and be sure they are on board, they've studied the papers, they're ready to start, before we can schedule, or should we schedule a date and then counsel calls and says, "Sorry, that's too soon for me, I'm not ready to start"? I'm not quite sure how you -- how to answer that question. This matter was postponed indefinitely precisely to enable the parties to find replacement counsel, and once replacement counsel is found, then this case will start, and provided that new counsel are ready to proceed. You understand the difficulty. So if you ask the Trial Chamber, "When is the trial going to start," so that new counsel can know, I just don't know how to answer that question. As for the second question, I guess you know as much as I do, that the length of the trial is anybody's guess at this stage until a 73 bis(C) decision has been made, there's no way of guesstimating the length of the trial, unless you can help me on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm fully aware of the questions that you have put just now. Of course, at this point in time, I do not think that I can tell a future colleague exactly what the situation would be. However, what would be helpful would be a tentative agreement on when the trial would start. Will it be this autumn, will it be a bit later, will it perhaps be next year? I think that this kind of information is very important. However, what I can say to you with certainty is that the colleagues I spoke to, and to whom General Markac spoke or, rather, he agrees that these persons can act as co-counsel, after we made them aware of the volume of material that we have available at this point in time, they all said that they would need about three months of preparation before a trial starts. However, I don't want to repeat myself. Nevertheless, it would be quite important, so that people could organise the work in their offices, because taking over a defence before The Hague Tribunal means that you stop working in your own office for at least a year. That is a rather long period, and therefore my colleagues would be more ready to agree if these basic parameters would be predictable, if not quite exact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to try and accommodate you, Mr. Mikulicic. Can we then suspend the discussion on conflict just for a moment and talk about when we think this trial might start? I'm inviting everybody to now join in on this one. It would seem to me as if the trial were said to be trial ready, it wouldn't be less than, you just said, three months, that the new counsel would need three months to prepare themselves. I would imagine that the trial would start in a period of five months from the time that people say they are ready. When that time when people say they are ready will come I am not able to say for the following reasons, and I would like us to think together around this. One, there is the possibility that this case may wait until I am ready to hear it. I'm currently starting a new case on Monday which is set to be -- which is expected to last just about a year. This case could also be taken out of our Chamber and be given to another Chamber, to be tried as soon as any other case within the Tribunal comes to an end. So those are the two possibilities that I see. I don't know when the first of the other cases will end. Now, I invite you to tell us, or to tell me also, how you think we should go around this question of determining how soon we think this case might begin. All I can say is if it's going to be heard by my Chamber, it's probably going to have to wait another year, starting tomorrow -- starting Monday. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I only raise not an original idea but one that was broached at the 65 ter conference, and that seemed to meet with some favourable response from the parties, and that was the possibility that instead of identifying a date certain for the commencement of trial, that the Trial Chamber indicated a date -- a sort of a minimum date, that the trial will not commence before a certain date. That tends to incorporate both of the elements the Court indicated, both the uncertainty of the actual starting date and the advisability of assisting the search for counsel by telling them, "You can be confident that you have the time to prepare and to arrange your personal and professional affairs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear that, and that report was given to me, Mr. Tieger. Now, I can only answer that question in relation to the possibility that this case will be heard by my Chamber. If it is taken out of this Chamber, then my answer would not be worth the paper it's written on. I am not able -- because any other case could collapse tomorrow and the President might say, "Gotovina case must start immediately." But if it is going to be heard by this Chamber, I say, in answer to your question, my Chamber is starting a new case on Monday, that case is expected to last a year, so -- and you know that that's also an estimation. It could be 10 months. From the developments of -- from yesterday in that case, it may also not begin on Monday. You know, it is just touch and go, everything. I don't know what's going to happen until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You appreciate my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The only thing I would add, and I know the Court has considered this also, is that in any event any other Trial Chamber would still face the reality that the Court mentioned earlier, and that is that counsel -- newly-appointed counsel would have to familiarise themselves with the case, and that imposes its own minimum, in any event, and it becomes almost paradoxical that the difficulty of imposing a minimum commencement date has any adverse impact on the ability to retain counsel when, in fact, it's that issue that, by itself, imposes a pragmatic minimum starting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to point out, as a technical matter, that the Appeals Chamber ruled on the Cermak conflict last Friday, and our interpretation of one portion of that decision is that the Appeals Chamber weighed the impact of the disqualification on the rights of General Cermak, and in that portion said that the trial is not likely to start for the next six months. So it may be that we already have some indication from the Appeals Chamber there about what the minimum period would be, and if we were to do it faster than that, there would of course be the question of how would that impact the Appeals Chamber's reasoning if, in fact, that turned out not to be true. So I guess it's -- I just throw that out there to remind the Trial Chamber that the Appeals Chamber has spoken on this point last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Misetic, and the six-month timeline is approximate -- is close to the five-month timeline that I gave a little earlier to say were we to decide now that we were going to try, it would take perhaps five months to begin the case, assuming that new counsel would need three months to acquaint themselves and whatever is outstanding in the pre-trial stage can be done, most probably five months, so it's the same thing as six months. Again, therefore, there are variables in answer to that question that was raised by Mr. Tieger. It could be five months, assuming we start now, or we can say it will be five months or six months from the time it is pronounced that the case is trial ready. So at least we can say it is not likely to start in the next six months. Now, the next question by Mr. Mikulicic is how long the trial will last. We tried to answer this problem -- this question so that he may be in a position to answer how soon they can get replacement counsel. I invite contributions on that. Mr. Tieger, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I respond because of the Court's invitation, but not because, and I hasten to be candid with the Court on this point, that I gave specific consideration to that issue before we stepped into court. I do recall that previously when the Court inquired, the Prosecution made a 12- to 14-month estimation, to the best of my recollection, assessing at that time the likelihood or at least the optimism at that point about the effort to reach agreed facts, streamline the case insofar as possible, and reach a point at which the genuinely-disputed issues in the case would be the focus of the trial. Nothing that has happened since that time has caused me to appreciably vary that estimate. I don't know what kind of precision the Trial Chamber may be looking for. I will say that at the time that estimate was given, it was given in the context of some of the institution's longer cases, that is, basically is this a two-year case, a three-year case and so on. So I wouldn't want it misinterpreted as imposing a level of precision either way. It may indeed be possible to -- and we would certainly strive to do so, to reduce the time. On the other hand, that may be an over-optimistic assessment. One of the issues raised at the 65 ter conference, as the Court is aware, was the efforts made by the parties to really identify what the facts in dispute are, and that effort is ongoing; but as an example of how potentially fruitful it is, is the fact that during a discussion about a related point that followed the 65 ter conference with my colleagues from the Gotovina Defence, we identified an issue that we all clearly thought could be the subject of a fruitful discussion that could eliminate a point that appeared to be in dispute but that, in reality, was not going to be in contention in a manner that would require much of the Court's time in trial. Sorry to be lengthy about that, but I just wanted it understood that was the previous estimate. I haven't looked at the case with an eye toward recalibrating that, but that's exactly what we've been trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you sit down, can I just ask you one or two questions. The 14-month estimate was based on the level of agreement on agreed facts at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Your Honour, there was -- that occurred long ago when the Court had received or -- either had directly received or was under the impression that the trial was a 22- to 24-month case. That was still at a time when I was relatively new to the case. My assessment at that time was that the case was amenable to a productive effort to streamline it, and through agreed facts and other means, and that a more realistic estimate, rather than the 22- to 24-month estimate was the 12- to 14-month estimate that I provided, so it assumed that agreed facts were to come, not based on any agreed facts that had been reached to date. Saying that, that doesn't mean that it was -- that I had in mind a specific list of agreed facts linked to specific witnesses who were to be called in the absence of those agreed facts. It was the best estimate based on my experience and the experience of my colleagues, so -- which is also part of why I built into this response some of the factors that led to that estimate. So I hope that's a helpful estimate, at least for Mr. Mikulicic, to the extent that my colleagues agree with it, and I think we all know that there's a plus-or-minus factor on that. But it seems to me that in this institution, when there are trials of extremely varying lengths, that that should be of some assistance in identifying where the Prosecution and/or the parties, as you'll hear from them, expect the case to be at the commencement of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's just get confirmation from the rest of your colleagues. Is that a realistic estimate still?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just have one clarification from the Prosecutor: Is the estimate of 12 to 14 months simply for the Prosecution case or is that idea encompassing the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to -- no, no, that was, again, and I can understand the question -- no, that was the case -- that was an estimate for the entirety of the case, assuming the best, in terms of the use of the mechanisms of efficiency provided by the Rules and agreed facts paring the case down to where the issues genuinely in dispute were the subject and focus of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, that had been my understanding also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just wanted that minor clarification of it, Your Honour. But I do believe that that's an actual estimate, given the factual agreements that we'll engaged in, I think that's approximately correct, 12 to 14 months. Give or take a little bit, as the Prosecutor noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Defence of General Cermak is asked to state its views about the date the trial goes ahead and how long it lasts, then I'd like to remind you of the notorious fact, and that is for logical conclusions to be made, you need the premises on the basis of which you're able to make those conclusions, and they should be certainly known. Now, with respect to the start of trial and the duration of trial, we don't have the necessary pre-conditions and premises which are certainly known. The Defence of General Cermak, or rather General Cermak who is left without a Defence team, does not know when he will be able to secure counsel for his defence, and we also do not know how long those new counsel will need to prepare the defence case. And another thing we don't know at this point in time is that we don't know which facts will be agreed upon. So all these questions remain open, and they will affect the duration of the trial and when the trial goes ahead. Of course, we will also respect the Court's ruling, because it is always up to the Court to decide when a trial goes to court and all other questions, and of course the dynamics of the trial would depend on all these other conditions. So I don't think that we can discuss this issue properly if we don't have all the facts, and therefore we cannot make a relevant conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, you're now making us dance in circles. Mr. Mikulicic suggested that we try to determine the start time and duration of the trial for him to be able to determine -- to answer his prospective colleagues who are likely to take over. Now you say now, for you to be able to determine the length of -- the duration of the trial and the start time, you must get replacement counsel. We're going backwards and forwards now. I understand that, and we will come to you and ask you when you think you can get replacement counsel, and we can deal with that at that stage. At this point in time, we're trying to deal with what is our best estimate of the duration of this trial, given that everybody is ready to go to trial, so that we can give an answer to Mr. Mikulicic in trying to help him to answer lawyers who are in Croatia. So can we deal with it on that basis, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, that's precisely what I'm talking about. You asked me about my opinion, so I am contributing to this discussion, not with a view to obstructing the proceedings, but what I'm doing, quite simply, is giving you some very realistic indices which it seems to me are making it impossible for us now to decide all these issues. As far as General Cermak's Defence is concerned, he received the ruling on the 29th of June, so of course he hasn't had sufficient time to seek new counsel. Now, how long he's going to need for that, if we look at how long he will take for that, if we look at General Markac's example, we can see it's not a very fast process; it might last a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, what the Chamber was asking you to comment on was to confirm or deny what the Prosecution was giving as its best estimate of the duration of the trial, as in when it starts, irrespective of when it starts, do you agree that a 12- to 14-month duration is a best estimate of this trial, whenever it will start? That's the question being put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that solves the problem, then let me say I agree straightaway, but I'm not quite sure that it will contribute to any of these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Mr. Mikulicic, do you also confirm the 14-month estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, viewing it from today's perspective and the evidence that has been disclosed thus far, I feel that that is a realistic estimate and that 14 months would be realistic for completion of trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, obviously that estimate takes into account the actual hearing of the case, and then thereafter there's judgement in writing, you can add another four months maybe, and that takes you to 18 months. Now, if we give you, as an answer to the questions that you asked initially, Mr. Mikulicic, that the trial is not likely to start at least within the next six months, and that when it does start, it might go for some 18 months, does that help you now to give answers to the prospective co-counsel that you are looking for? Does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Those are facts which are fairly exact and, on the basis of which, one can draw conclusions and talk to a potential candidate for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Now, having been given those answers, are you able to answer the question that was put to you earlier as to how soon you think you are likely to get replacement counsel? We are going back now to conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With these parameters, that is to say, that the trial will start, counting from today's date, in six months' time, brings us to the beginning of next year, and along with the fact that the trial could last for about 18 months, as Your Honour has just stated, I feel that we could inform the Court about the selection of counsel right after the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulicic. That's quite helpful. Let me just make one little clarification. We didn't say the trial will start in six months. We said at least for the next six months, it will not start. That seems to be fairly certain. It could be longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that fully. But in view of the circumstances, we don't know, as you say, exactly when it will start, but we can say when it will not start. So within the frameworks of those parameters, I said what I said with respect to the new replacement counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay, we will then try to find out from you, by the end of the summer recess, what progress you have made in that regard. May we then move on, unless somebody has any comments to make on Mr. Separovic's position. Any comments? Nothing. Okay. Can we move on to Prodanovic and Ms. Slokovic's conflict of interest. The Appeal Chamber again decided on the 29th of June to uphold the Trial Chamber's decision on conflict of interest on the 15th of April. The Trial Chamber's decision set forth in paragraph 25 that Mr. Prodanovic and Mrs. Slokovic are required to stay on until new counsel can satisfy that he, she, or they can take over the case. Even though it has only been one week since the appeals decision is out, I trust that Mr. Cermak is already working on finding new counsel and that Mr. Prodanovic and Mrs. Slokovic will inform the Trial Chamber in due course when new counsel has been found. But having said that, if you do have anything that you can tell us at this stage, Mr. Prodanovic, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart what I've already said, no, Your Honour, I have nothing to add. We will inform you in due course as soon as we have concrete results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Anybody else got anything to say on that? Mr. Tieger, Mr. Kehoe? Nothing? Okay. Thank you very much. Can we then move on to the position of Mr. Kehoe's alleged conflict of interest. Now, this issue was raised on the 13th of April, 2007, in Mr. Cermak and Mr. Markac's joint motion which resulted in the Trial Chamber's order to the Registrar regarding Gregory Kehoe's appointment as Defence counsel for Ante Gotovina on the 25th of June, 2007. The Registrar's response is due to be filed by Monday, the 10th of July of 2007. On the basis of that response and any replies the parties may wish to file further, the Trial Chamber will issue a decision in due course. Do the parties have anything to add on this at this point? Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then a decision will be rendered fairly soon. The question of agreed facts. I know we've touched on them a little bit this afternoon, but in the last status conference the parties agreed that there was a framework within which they could discuss agreed facts and that they needed to focus on the logistics so that this process could begin to materialise. It was proposed that the agreed facts make efforts to cover, amongst others, facts and crime-based evidence including evidence on the accused's various positions, victims' lists and the identity of victims, exhumation evidence and applicable law. Is there any progress report that we can get on this? We'll start with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to summarise what the Court may already be familiar with as a result of the briefing related to the 65 ter. But in respect of logistics and focus, first of all, I think the factors the Court identified or the areas of focus the Court identified were shared by the parties. We began in particular with one of those in terms of logistics. The Prosecution prepared materials in hard copy for the parties so that it wouldn't be a question of gathering the materials or a risk that the parties weren't talking about the same matters, based on the same documents, and disseminated them. These are materials related to the scheduled killings, forensic materials, and pertinent witness statements; and it is these materials that have been the subject of discussions, the most recent of which focused on the notion of a schedule or matrix, kind of a checklist, if you will, of the sub-issues arising from that so that, one at a time, the parties could say, "With respect to this issue arising from the forensic materials, there's no dispute," or,"there is a dispute," let's focus on that, see what the nature of the dispute is and so on. The matter was raised by Mr. Pitman at the 65 ter, and the responses from counsel appeared to be heartening, in the sense that having looked at those materials specifically, as the parties have had a chance to do, there were indications that for at least a good part of the material, agreement was expected. Now, having said that, everyone acknowledged the problem, that we don't have all counsel in the case to agree on the facts, and that, unmistakably, is a bit of a problem. Nevertheless, we clearly didn't want to defer any effort to begin the process until such time as counsel came on. First of all, we can make progress in terms of the process, if nothing else, and there's reason to believe that any tentative agreements arrived at by the parties in this context will hopefully be shared by the subsequent counsel, or at least they'll have a head start when we make the effort to finalise the areas of agreement. So that's the logistical process and how it's gone forward. That's the -- a summary, anyway, encapsuled summary, of what's happened on that. One more factor is that that's not the -- those are not the only issues we've been discussing, but they are the issues we've been discussing in the most concrete terms in the manner I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation, Mr. Tieger. Just before I go to other counsel, what's your answer, in a word? Are the parties making good progress in finalising agreed facts or are there problems? Just in a sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wouldn't call the progress good at this point. There's a lot of -- there seems to be a lot of goodwill. I can't identify a particular sticking point. The materials were disseminated some time ago, and the progress on those specific points has not been remarkably impressive since then, but they are voluminous and they do raise various issues, and maybe there's a point of critical mass and we're just now about to hit it. The parties have had a chance to -- the Defence has had a chance to absorb materials, read them carefully, and maybe that's an inevitable period that doesn't reflect any serious problem but just the need to review those materials. But indeed I wish I was in a position to say to the Court, "Here are the concrete results from that discussion." That's part of the reason this schedule was suggested, so that we can say, "Look, here are the specific points arising from this. What's the answer to whether or not there's agreement on this particular point with respect to these particular materials and these particular incidents?" So I don't want to mislead the Court into thinking that the efforts I described by themselves are enough to result in an expedited case, but it has seriously begun. And I hope that because the materials have been in these concrete and hard copy materials -- have been in the hands of the Defence for some time, that now we're in a position to really finalise this checklist and move on to the next issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Anything further? Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that the whole idea of the schedule, with talking about the homicides, is very important to shaving or reducing time at trial. Many of these homicide counts, and just for the ones that are listed in the indictment, which there are 37 of them or 36 of them, require analysis on a case-by-case basis to go into things like identification, location, manner of death, manner of -- where the burial was, ethnicity, who if anyone is identified as possible. And if we put this out on a schedule, a matrix, whatever you want to call it, we can identify, okay, in Homicide 4 we, hypothetically speaking, we have this particular issue that we need to address. And there are many of those issues that we need not address. Now, as we continue on on this process, which takes a little time at the beginning because of the critical mass, it will move more quickly as time goes on, because not only are we addressing the homicides that are in the actual indictment, there is also another list that was given on the clarification document sent by counsel which now I believe it adds up to approximately 237 or 238 murders or homicides that need to be addressed. That being said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is asked to slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That being said, it is a very, very, very beneficial use of time, because what we can do is highlight what specific point on what particular murder charge needs to be litigated and brought before the Court. And that is going to be an enormous time-saver when we don't have to get into all the other details that a normal homicide case might have to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just say at this point to both you and Mr. Tieger, thank you very much, and I do appreciate that as tedious as this process may be, it is eventually going to be time-saving at trial. But the question for now is whether this tedious process, is it making progress. Are you making progress in that direction, in coming to agreement on agreed facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The answer to that question is "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, any contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really have nothing special to add to what my colleagues have already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, this has to do with forensic information that is rather accurate and precise, but voluminous, too. I think that once we've had a look at this, we will be able to agree on most of the forensics, if I can put it that way, and in this way we will contribute to expediting the trial. I have nothing else to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add one other factor which may be encouraging? And I take it it came from a rather brief discussion with Mr. Tieger, and of course some of the evidence going to be presented by the Defence had to do with evidence that Your Honour heard in the Martic case, without going into the specifics of that, but some of that evidence is going to be presented again here. And after a brief discussion with Mr. Tieger, we essentially have come to agreement on much of that, and that will cut out a tremendous amount of time. So merely getting into this discussion and we didn't set out to address that particular issue, it just happened during the course of discussions after the 65 ter conference this morning. So I am encouraged when we are together and we do begin to move down this path together, that we will make significant progress and more so as time goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kehoe. And while you're on that point of a chance meeting after the 65 ter meeting which has made you so hopeful, may I just remind the parties that at the last status conference there had been mention of drawing up a schedule of regular meetings between the parties precisely to promote this process. May I suggest that rather than these chance meetings after 65 ter meetings, we have these scheduled meetings specifically to address these issues, particularly now that we have an idea that at least in the next six months we're not likely to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I think that's a very good idea. To the extent that we have not done that, I bear as much negligence as anybody else in that regard. We have talked about this and there are e-mails going back and forth. I hasten to add that having specific meetings on that score might not be productive until new counsel comes in so they can participate as well, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I differ on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to suggest that if you can carry on, it's much easier for incoming counsel to review what you've agreed on and just to say,"I agree with this one," "I disagree with that one," "I agree with this one," "I disagree with that one," rather than to start the whole process. I would urge the parties to please not postpone this process until you get counsel on both. I would urge the parties to please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, we will be guided by that wisdom, Judge, and if I can turn to my colleague, he would like to mention an item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did want to point out that the Gotovina Defence, in addition to the homicide issues, we are preparing a long schedule of the entire case in terms of what facts can be agreed upon. But we would like to do is, as soon as new counsel is on board, first distribute among members of our colleagues on the Defence side, get agreement on what facts the defendants will all agree on, because I think a precondition is that all of the defendants agree to stipulate the certain facts before we tender it to the Prosecution, and then jointly tender that document and see what we exactly can agree upon. But we are working intensively on all facts in this entire case. I don't want the Court to think that we're working on just homicides, and in addition to that, as Mr. Kehoe said, we believe that the Martic stipulations will cut out a lot of the background facts so that we can save some time there. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Misetic. For that contribution, it's appreciated. I underline once again the need for scheduled meetings between the parties to promote the process. And I urge the parties to please not wait until counsel -- new counsel is on board before those meetings are undertaken. Are there any further contributions on this topic? Mr. Prodanovic, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we move on to the next item, which is motions under Rules 92 bis and 92 ter. After the last status conference and the Prosecution's motion for extension of time to file these motions under these Rules, the Trial Chamber granted the request for the Prosecution and invited it to indicate when the Trial Chamber should expect such motions. On the 10th of May, the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber that it intended to file these motions once a trial date is set. The Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecution should start to file these motions now, before a trial date is set. It will have the opportunity -- I mean, the Prosecution will have the opportunity to amend the motions if the circumstances of these witnesses should change in the meantime, and I would like to urge you, the Prosecution, to start filing these motions. And I don't know whether you have any comments to make, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That was raised by Mr. Pitman at the 65 ter and discussed, and I believe we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Are you able to give yourselves a timeline?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was one of the issues raised. I would be disinclined to do so at the moment. What we understand from the discussions at the 65 ter, and I'll express my understanding of that and the Court can indicate whether that's correct, the Court was clear that it wanted those motions filed -- wanted the Prosecution not to wait until the trial date was set, but at the same time it was disinclined to impose a specific date. I indicated that at this point shortly before the recess, with various -- and we have a number of things scheduled, for example, 92 bis missions, or missions for that purpose, it would be -- and then we have various people who are significant to that process leaving in connection with the court recess, that I would be -- I would ask the Court not to impose a specific and immediate deadline. We'll look at the matter as quickly as possible, try to get back to the Court before the recess with some indication of the time, and in full appreciation of the fact that the Court would obviously like the Prosecution to start filing 92 bis motions well in advance of the scheduling of the trial date. So we understand that the Court doesn't want a delay. We'd like to get this out of the way, and furthermore would like to have some indication of when those are going to be filed, and I'm just asking for some tolerance in how quickly we let the Court know what that rough sketch that will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tieger. I think there isn't any substantial difference between what you've just said and my understanding of the report of the 65 ter meeting. My understanding was that the Prosecution had asked for a timeline, but suggested that it not be earlier than before the summer recess. Now, certainly you can be assured we are not imposing any timeline before the summer recess, but now our question really to you was that you impose a timeline on yourself rather than it being imposed by us. In other words, give us an estimate by when you think you can begin to file these motions. I want you to tie yourself, I don't want you to be tied by the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that, Your Honour, and if the Court will give me an opportunity to meet with the members of my team and get back to the Court, we'll certainly do so before the summer recess and then start filing those motions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just as a reminder from the last status conference, it had been suggested to the Prosecution that these motions will be sub-filed in bundles, in other words, not a motion per person but a motion for a group of people, each one motivated in the motion, but so that we don't have many motions to deal with but we can deal with one motion dealing with a number of people at a time. Okay, thank you very much. Any comments from other members of the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic? Nothing. Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulicic. Do we then move on to the questions of disclosure. May I say that the question of disclosure should also not be impeded by issues relating to counsel or the pending motion regarding Mr. Kehoe's alleged conflict. I would suggest this question of disclosure carries on. In the last status conference, the Prosecution had indicated that the hyper-linked exhibit list was being completed and that it was able to provide to the Defence every document mentioned on the exhibit list on a disc. Some documents omitted from the exhibit list but referenced in the Pre-Trial Brief were also on this disc. These were to be considered supplemental to the exhibit list. I just want to find out whether the Defence can confirm that they are in receipt of all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, there are some ministerial issues going back and forth and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ministerial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ministerial on numbering and things of that nature, but, Your Honour, the disclosure has been going pretty well, and with these many documents there are going to be a few misses along the way. And we've been talking to the Office of the Prosecutor and taking care of those issues, so the bottom line is we don't have any complaints at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have received the documents, and we have nothing special to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prodanovic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our position is the same. We have nothing special to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, the Prosecution had also said that a small number of statements were still pending translation and their translation should have been completely shortly after the last status conference. Is that the case now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And they've been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Can we then focus specifically on the Rule 70 disclosure. At the last conference, again, the Prosecution stated that one of the principal providers had cleared a significant number of documents and that within a week all this information would be disclosed to the Defence. Was this done?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge. I mean, I believe that referred -- I'm trying to reconstruct that. I think that referred to a particular provider, and if I'm correct about that, yes, that was done, as anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was -- what had to be done was within a week of the last status conference, all this information would be disclosed to the Defence. My question is: Has that disclosure been made to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to double-check that. There may be one document among many that I haven't -- that I'm not certain about. But with that exception -- another document hasn't been disclosed, but another document that hasn't been cleared, but all the cleared documents which, as I indicate, are the vast majority if not all of the documents that have been cleared, have of course been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand you. One document has not been cleared?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's the case. I'm double-checking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're waiting for it to be cleared before you can disclose it. But otherwise everything else has been cleared that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of those documents that were the subject of the Court's inquiry at the last status conference, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask, are there any other outstanding documents that have not yet been cleared?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give an indication of how soon you think they will be cleared?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Some indication. There are -- we received clearance on approximately 250 of those documents, and those are in the process of being disclosed, that is, the mechanics of disclosing them are happening, and they will be disclosed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you? My question is: Of the uncleared documents, how soon do you hope to receive clearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The only way I can be certain of that, Your Honour, is to double-check with the providers. I am -- that is, and we do that periodically, is to re-contact the providers, indicate that we're waiting and the Court is waiting, and urge them to expedite the process insofar as possible. Beyond that, I don't have any specific indications by the providers of when they will be cleared. But based on the Court's inquiry, we'll undertake efforts to motivate the providers insofar as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber will appreciate that very much. Thank you so much. Are you able to confirm receipt of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, obviously this is -- I take -- we have received some Rule 70 and we just take it on faith from the Prosecution that they're going through the process of taking it. We don't know what's there, obviously, so I just rely on their good faith, which they have demonstrated throughout, so we'll just move on from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I'm asking is what they interpret to have delivered to you, they have delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you confirm that, Mr. Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Apparently at the 65 ter conference this morning, there was mention of 13 witnesses and some -- statements of 13 witnesses and expert reports that are outstanding. Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have a list of 13 witnesses which we have discussed with the Prosecution. Some of them, I believe, are fact witnesses that we don't have the statements for and I will follow up with Mr. Tieger afterwards on them. Some of them, one of them is a -- is the Rule 70 witness I think we were talking about just prior to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Some of it deals with -- the rest of it deals with expert witnesses, and the issue there is some of them have prepared reports but have no statements, and so I think at this point Mr. Tieger indicated that if they have given us just the statement -- just the report, then there is no statement. However, some of the experts that they have identified have not yet prepared reports, is my understanding. And so having thought about it after the 65 ter conference, the only thing we wish to avoid is a situation where we don't have -- we get expert reports on the eve of trial, and obviously from the Defence perspective, the sooner those reports can be prepared and tendered to us, the faster we can move on the process of maybe perhaps agreeing to the facts in that report, hiring our own experts on those matters, et cetera, so that does seem to be an open issue that we didn't discuss at the 65 ter, quite frankly, because I didn't have time to think it through then, but that would be the only issue right now that I guess is still open, and that's with respect to expert reports -- experts that have been identified but have not yet prepared reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Misetic. Do you have any comments to make on that, Mr. Tieger, particularly on the expert reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I understand Mr. Misetic's concern about receiving reports on the eve of trial. I indicated to him that to some extent there's a small chicken-and-egg problem, but we'll resolve that through discussions and through efforts. That involves the extent to which agreed facts may implicate the need for particular issues to be addressed by an expert, and also the issue of ongoing efforts by the Prosecution to obtain documents that it has been seeking for some time that bear on the expert reports. Having said that, we do keep in mind the timing and the need for sufficient -- submissions in sufficient time before trial to not impede the trial process, but we have been and will continue to be in good communication with the Defence so that I don't think that issue is likely to arise. We'll keep this issue on the agenda and keep discussing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'll have noticed by now that this Chamber would like timelines. You know, the promise to continue to do things in good faith, welcome as it may be, is really just a little something -- it's some fairy-airy kind of promise and it doesn't give a sense of by when things will be done and how ready can this case be ready for trial. And I understand your difficulty, having said that, that this is maybe an area where -- first of all, you said it's a chicken-and-egg situation. Secondly, it's partly out of your control, in the sense that you referring to also these Rule 70 disclosures which still have to be cleared. But be that as it may, let me do what was done to the Chamber this afternoon and just ask for a rough estimate about how soon we think these things can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all for clarification purposes, it's not a matter of the Rule 70 documents, which is a matter outside our control, as you noted, but it's also a matter of documents which we have been requesting from archival sources for a long time that have not been made available, and we have doubled and redoubled our efforts to obtain them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question on that one. Having asked for this information from archival sources for a long time, and redoubled your efforts, do you still have any hope of getting those materials?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The documents are significant enough, Your Honour, and our determination to get them is substantial enough that I do retain that hope and I won't abandon those efforts. Now, the only -- I realise that there is an ultimate deadline for that that is exclusive to that effort and has nothing to do with the effort to obtain the documents or the likelihood to obtain the documents, and that's the trial date, and so I have to back it up from then. Now, when we come to a point that begins to implicate the commencement of trial, the Defences' ability to prepare and deal with the documents that we'll be submitting, then we have to impose a deadline, irrespective of the success of those efforts. And I should say we may be asking the Court at some point to assist with those efforts if they're not successful. At this point, we're pursuing them as vigorously as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you talk of imposing a deadline, imposing it on who, on the archival sources or on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On ourselves for the preparation and submission of those -- calling it a deadline for the submission of those reports. I realise they're not linked forever exclusively to the issues I've just identified, they're ultimately linked to the commencement of trial, and I appreciate that. I think at the moment we need to continue making those efforts so the reports are as focused and useful as possible. And I would be in a position to give the Court a more definitive date for the submission of the report if those issues were resolved, and they're not. Having said that, I appreciate the fact that the Court wants to be assured that the commencement of trial is not jeopardised, wants to be assured that the Defence's opportunity to prepare is not undermined and therefore has some concern about those submission dates, but I don't think we're in that area of risk yet. That's one reason I mentioned discussions with the Defence. They want to be apprised of the relative progress and the dates by which they'll be receiving reports of expert witnesses, but at this moment I don't think those considerations militate in favour of a specific submission date in the immediate future. And I know there will come a point when that happens, and maybe by the next status conference we'll need to set a certain date, I think it is three or four months hence, it may be before then and the Defence will say that, and if necessary we will raise it with the Court before the status conference. But at the moment, I can't put a particular date on it, and I don't see any external factors which necessitate it for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one little point. You alluded to, at some point, maybe approaching the Court for assistance. Don't you think maybe this is about time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's close, Your Honour, but I think there are still one or two steps that -- well, I'll revisit the issue with the Court's suggestion in mind. We anticipated there's still a few more steps that we anticipated undertaking in pursuit of that effort, and again I'll revisit that to see if it's more appropriate to take it before the Court or more effective to complete those steps first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. May I just say that try to bear in mind approaching the Court as soon as you possibly can if there is anything that the Court can do. Thank you very much. Mr. Misetic, you indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one matter on this score. To some degree with regard to this, and if it's going to impact the indictment and, you know, there's another motion pending to alter the indictment in several fashions, and if it goes to expert testimony, I don't know how long it's going to take to come up with any expert to counter the expert that the Prosecution might put up once they get these documents in hand. We're talking about a lot of chickens and eggs here, but of course that's an issue that comes to mind, I mean, and that's going to be somewhat protracted. So I would urge the Office of the Prosecutor to bring any issues concerning -- now, keeping in mind that this case has been going on for 12 years, urge any issue concerning the getting of documents be brought before the Court now, and let's get on with it, for lack of a better terminology. I understand their efforts, et cetera, but any effort to move this along should be sooner as opposed to later, especially if the Court has got to intercede and there is some timeline before this archival entity has got to respond. I mean, how long does that take? I don't know either, Judge, and it's purely hypothetical at this point, but I would urge this to move more quickly before the Court and bring it before the Court more quickly as opposed to waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to point out that this topic could be quite problematic. If the expert reports are tied to their archival problems and if the issue -- I'm sorry for having to be cryptic because I can't speak to what their subject is, but if their subject is what I think it is, it's a very material matter to this case which, from the Defence perspective, will involve more than just hiring an expert. It will involve a lot of fieldwork on that problem, and it's a subject of dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence to this point. I wanted to point out to the Court that for that reason, it really could have a long-term impact on our ability to say we're ready for trial, if we get these reports in January, February or March of next year. The one other thing was I think the Court is aware from the 65 ter conference that I raised a matter concerning precisely archives, and I don't know if the Court wants me to address that now or wait until we get to other matters. I think it's probably related, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've got it to deal with it later, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unless you say it's inextricably intertwined with these issues we're talking about right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we raised the matter of the archive, and it is related to Croatian State Archives, so they're linked issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's a question of access. Can we deal with it a little later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All I can say to you, Mr. Tieger, is as I urged you to approach the Court as soon as you possibly can, you hear what your colleagues are saying, they're endorsing what I said, and I can't say it in more stronger words than I've said. Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add to that. We agree with the position of General Gotovina's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honour. However, I wish to add that today, with our colleagues from the Prosecution, we exchanged views and we told them what some of our objections were in relation to 65 ter disclosures until now, and we are trying to deal with these minor technical problems and we hope that we will succeed soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulicic. Can we then deal with the question of pending motions? On the 26th of March, 2007, the Gotovina Defence filed the motion pursuant to Rule 73, requesting the Pre-trial Chamber to strike part of the Prosecution's Pre-Trial Brief, constituting effective amendment of the joinder indictment. The Prosecution's response was filed on the 10th of April, 2007, and the Gotovina motions for leave to file a reply and the reply were filed on the 17th of April. A decision will be handed down fairly shortly in that respect. I don't know whether the parties have anything to say. Nothing. Nothing. Mr. Prodanovic. Nothing. Thank you very much. Now, on the 17th of May, 2007, the Prosecution filed the motion to amend the indictment, and on the 31st of May, 2007, Gotovina's response was filed. The Prosecution's motion for leave to reply and reply was filed on the 7th of June, and Mr. Gotovina's response was filed on the 11th of June. The decision in this issue will be handed down before the summer recess. Any comments? No comment, no comment. On the 1st of June, 2007, the Trial Chamber issued an order to the Prosecutor under Rule 77 to investigate whether there was sufficient bases to proceed with a contempt of court case under Rule 77 under the Rules following the leaking of a confidential filing to and by the Croatian press. The Trial Chamber has not been informed of what the status of this investigation is. I'm told that this morning the Prosecution indicated that it hadn't done anything because it is awaiting a decision on the motion on amicus -- amicus prosecutor. Maybe we might just get a clarification from the rest of the parties. You don't have any further filings you want to make on this issue; is that why you want the decision to be made under amicus?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have no further filing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the amicus --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Intended, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You filed the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Mikulicic, you have no filing? Mr. Prodanovic, you have no filing? In that event then, a decision will be rendered before the summer recess. Again on the same day counsel for General Gotovina filed a motion for the appointment of an amicus curiae instead of the OTP, again we will render a decision on that as well, okay. It's the same thing, okay. Things that are listed as coming under "General" which came from this morning's 65 ter meeting conference were: The trial start date, which we have already discussed; the question of Mr. Markac's testimony in the Ademi trial on the 16th of July. Can we deal with that, please? What is the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course you know that my client is on provisional release and that he is bound to act according to the rules set out in the decision made by the Trial Chamber. However, there are proceedings underway in Zagreb, proceeding that were referred to Zagreb according to Rule 11 bis against Generals Norac and Ademi, and the Court called General Markac as a witness in these proceedings. His testimony would be public, in public session. This gives rise to a few questions, or rather these questions are put by General Markac's Defence. Question number one: What is the position of this Trial Chamber with regard to such public testimony, and in terms of the constraints imposed by the Trial Chamber when deciding on provisional release, as far as General Markac is concerned? Question number 2: If such a statement were to be made by General Markac, does it previously have to be approved by this Trial Chamber, since he is under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, if I can put it that way? This is what my own thinking on this is: If General Markac were not provisionally released, if he were in detention of this Tribunal, then the Zagreb Court would certainly have to seek permission from the Tribunal for this kind of testimony. I think, by way of an analogy, that in this case, when General Markac is provisionally released, although there are some constraints involved, again permission should be sought from this Trial Chamber for this kind of testimony. There is another group of questions that invariably appears here, and that is the question of using General Markac's statement before this court in Zagreb and whether it would be used in the trial before this Tribunal. General Markac, at least in the present-day situation, he is not prepared to testify before this Trial Chamber. What would the probative value be in that case of his testimony before the Zagreb Court in relation to the evidence in these proceedings? Question number 3: If General Markac were to testify before the Zagreb Court, he may touch upon certain circumstances that could be incriminating for him in relation to the material that is presented before this Trial Chamber, so it seems to me -- and therefore we kindly ask this Trial Chamber to take a position on this and to instruct us, in a way, as to how we should react with regard to this case. Obviously, the question is a very serious one. I will be glad to answer any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulicic. You're asking very involved and difficult questions, some of which I'm not sure whether belong at the door of this Trial Chamber or belong at the door of counsel to give legal advice to his client. But to cut a long story short, and I say this mindful of the fact that Mr. Markac is expected to testify on the 16th, but I just want to say, to cut a long story short: Can I suggest that you give -- you file a short motion, just short motivations on these issues, and let the Trial Chamber deal with them in that manner, rather than try to get an answer here which may or may not be properly thought through. Would that be helpful?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that would certainly be helpful. However, this is what I would like to suggest: That what I said today in respect of public testimony to be given by General Markac and questions related thereto should be treated as an oral motion with regard to this particular question. If you wish, of course, we can repeat this in writing, but that is time-consuming, after all. Today is Friday, so we can do that only next Monday or Tuesday, and the 16th is getting closer and closer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, and I'm suggesting what I'm suggesting mindful of that, Mr. Mikulicic. If you get it on Monday, we'll try to give you a decision soon enough to be on time for the 16th. Okay, thank you very much. Then there was the issue raised by the Gotovina Defence relating to access to Croatian State archives. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This relates to the matter that I had raised earlier with the Court. We believe there is an issue with respect to the due process rights of the defendants and their rights to equality of arms. By way of background, all the parties in this case use the Croatian State Archives by necessity in order to prepare their cases, both Prosecution and Defence. In addition to parties in this case, parties in other cases before this Tribunal, including cases from Bosnian and Herzegovina, use the Croatian State Archive. There are prescribed rules that the Croatian State Archive imposes as to what times the parties can access the archive, the means of accessing the archive, the means of photocopying and the fact that we bear the cost of those copying expenses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are those rules --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Apply to everyone, correct, they are unilaterally applied to all equally. So over the course of the past 16 months, we have diligently worked in the Croatian State Archive to get our case to where it is today, and have incurred perhaps tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of kunas in expense in photocopying, et cetera to get those documents for this particular case. It came to the attention of the Gotovina Defence several weeks ago that there was an issue with the Prosecution gaining access to those archives, and it was information, and I leave it as could be true, could not be true, I don't have any firsthand knowledge of it, but that the Prosecution was seeking greater access than the rules that apply to everyone else. And to that end, what we find particularly objectionable is that the Prosecutor referred to this problem in her address to the Security Council, concerning problems in particular and by name referencing the Gotovina case and that she was having difficulties obtaining documents from the Croatian State Archives in the Gotovina case in particular. The result of that is a potential for misuse in the sense that the political pressure that is exerted on the Croatians to comply, for reasons related to their -- for their own political reasons, could result in a situation where the Prosecution gets favours and privileges that don't apply to everyone else, and I wanted just to bring that to the attention of the Trial Chamber and point out that it's our position that in addressing matters involving state compliance, Rule 7 bis I think is quite clear that it is this Trial Chamber that has the jurisdiction to resolve matters involving state compliance, including compliance with disclosure of documents. I think that jurisdiction is exclusive, and that is the only way to safeguard the due-process rights of the defendants, because obviously we would have a right to comment on any situation where they were requesting documents, and quite frankly to seek equal treatment so that if the Prosecution gains - and speaking hypothetically now - 24-hour access to the Croatian State Archives and we have five hours a day, we would invite the Trial Chamber, to the extent that an order would be issued, that we gain the same rights and access to those archives that any other party to the case would have. That ability to put our case forward and ask for those rights is circumvented when the Prosecutor goes directly to the Security Council to address her concerns rather than using Rule 7 bis to resolve those issues, and so we would invite the Trial Chamber to invite the parties to use the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Statutes of the Tribunal in resolving issues related to the disclosure of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the relief you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asking the Trial Chamber to tell the Prosecution to desist from approaching the Security Council with respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to document disclosure issues from state sources, and that those should be addressed through the procedures outlined -- right, by name it was mentioned. This was not a situation where she was referring to Croatians cooperation with the Tribunal generally, but by name, in this case, and we believe that usurped the jurisdiction of this Trial Chamber, because it is this Trial Chamber, under Rule 7 bis, that resolves issues of state compliance. And by the way what is significant for us is it gives us the right, when Rule 7 bis is used, to file a response and to ask for relief or to comment on the request. When political means are used, rather than judicial means to resolve these problems, it directly implicates the rights of the accused under Article 21 of the Statute, we believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
