utterances.text: I'll be quick and, I hope -- well, I hope I'll be quick and I hope it will be simple. First of all, to the extent that the Defence has had any difficulties with either access or obtaining documents, we can only sympathise, because I alluded to similar problems before. With respect to the issue -- with respect to the matter of favours and privileges, the Prosecution seeks no favours and privileges. It only seeks the full access to archives and the full rights to which it's entitled, and fully shares the view that all the parties in the case should have equal and unfettered access to archival materials, to whatever extent it may be bound by legitimate logistical considerations. The Prosecutor has an obligation, insofar as I understand it, and this is not something I've recently researched, to report to the Security Council on matters such as cooperation. I alluded a few -- so that's something that the Prosecutor does and should do, and should be expected to do. And the issue of whether or not there has been full cooperation is one I alluded to earlier, back in this very court, in indicating to the Court that we were having trouble in obtaining documents. That is a matter properly, it seems to me, brought to the attention of the Security Council and is not a matter of seeking favours and privileges. I'm more than happy to see my colleagues from the Defence and all parties in this litigation or any other litigation have the most complete access possible. To the extent the Prosecution has in the past or will in the future identify any inappropriate barriers to our access, we'll raise them. And if indeed that results in the elimination of unnecessary bureaucratic obstacles, we trust that the Defence will be able to benefit similarly from the elimination of such inappropriate obstacles. So that's all I have to add. I don't see how that's implicated by the Prosecutor's ongoing, wholly appropriate and, I think, necessary report to the Security Council about the cooperation among -- by member states with the OTP and the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I just comment on that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would respectfully disagree with my colleague. Rule 7 bis(a) specifically says and establishes what the procedure is, and the Security Council is only made aware after the Trial Chamber is satisfied that a state has failed to comply with an obligation under Article 29 which relates to any proceeding before that Chamber, the Chamber or Judge may advise the President, who shall report the matter to the Security Council. The Rule is clear, it is not in the jurisdiction of the Prosecutor to be unilaterally and ex parte, in fact, contacting the Security Council for assistance in resolving the matter. It requires that you, the Chamber, first be satisfied and then the President eventually to report the matter to the Security Council, so I would disagree on that point. As a matter of practicality and how this really applies, the fact of the matter is the parties for the most part don't know and are not courtesy-copied on requests to various states for documents, so there's really no way of the Defence knowing generally what prerogatives or privileges or, let's put it this way, removal of bureaucratic obstacles, which certainly exists for the defendants as well, there's no way of us knowing that those obstacles have been removed unless the Prosecution would copy us every time they put in a document request and told us what had been done, which obviously not only isn't done but isn't required to be done by the parties. Therefore, as a general matter, I think it's important that because we both don't know what each other are doing, that we respect the Rule, which is if we have a problem and we believe it's of a sufficient degree to require assistance from the Chamber in gaining the compliance of a state to obtain information, we will certainly proceed pursuant to Rule 7 bis to obtain that. We don't have the ability to contact the Security Council and ask for relief. It's an imbalance in the powers, the respective powers. It results in an inequality. And equality is guaranteed under Article 21 under the Statute. That equality of arms can only be guaranteed if Rule 7 bis is respected, and so again we would ask that in the future, that matters related to a particular case -- I should say in this particular case, concerning state cooperation, should be brought pursuant to the explicit Rule to the attention of the Chamber, and then if the matter is so significant that it requires a report to the Security Council, that matter should then be addressed by the President and not the Prosecutor. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You're talking of the future, Mr. Misetic. I'm not quite sure whether, when you say so, you are saying you are just putting this on record, you are not pursuing it unless it happens again, or are you actually seeking specific redress from this Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we have heard -- again, the problem is I don't know what the Prosecution is doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have heard today that the Prosecution has problems gaining access to archives and intends to use some other means before resorting to moving to the Trial Chamber, so I think the matter is ripe at the moment because, again, I don't know what the other means are. To the extent they are political, extra-judicial means, I think it would be our request that an invitation be made by the Chamber that if there is a problem, that judicial means be used to resolve that and not extra-judicial/political means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that you formalise this question by another motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess we can then go beyond -- past it, unless you had something to add on to this motion, Mr. Prodanovic or Mr. Mikulicic. Yes, Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, are you asking me about my position on what is being presented or what? I didn't understand you. The Defence of General Cermak does not see any great problem here. We consider this to be an unnecessary parade, because certainly a solution to the situation of whether possibly the Prosecutor, in an unauthorised manner, skipped the President of the Tribunal and contacted the Security Council herself first will not be the first or last time, and I think this is a problem that isn't really relevant and does not exist, per se, and isn't relevant to the case. I think there are far greater problems that need to be addressed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prodanovic. Mr. Mikulicic, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wholeheartedly join in what Mr. Prodanovic has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the matter will rest there. Can we then move to the question of assistance to the new team that I'm told was raised by Mrs. Slokovic this morning at the 65 ter conference. I'm told for the tapes we have to last five minutes, and this is the last item.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all I wanted was to ask the Trial Chamber or rather you to explain to us which our authorisations are they in during the transition, that is to say, what are the authorisations of the Defence, are they complete and full? Do we wholeheartedly participate in the proceedings which come prior to the introduction of the new Defence counsel or are there certain restrictions, limitations? So can we participate in the proceedings to harmonise and dovetail matters with respect to the facts, agreement on facts? Can we take part in that in an active way instead of the Defence team coming in? Can we agree on facts and on the basis of that, can we put the new Defence team in front of a fate accompli, and is it possible for that -- should that be a reason for them -- or rather can they deviate from any conclusions or decisions made by us with respect to those facts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your question, Mrs. Slokovic, but let me say this: I guess the decision was quite clear that the current team will stay on until the new team has taken over and certified that they are on board. Once that has happened, you and Mr. Prodanovic will be expected to get off the team. Until then, you carry on acting as full counsel for your client. That's my understanding. Let me make it clear. You see, no situation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your situation is different from Mr. Separovic's situation, because in your situation the entire team is being removed. So the decision said you will stay on until new counsel is on, and for the time that you are on, you will act with full powers of counsel, whereas in the case of Mr. Separovic, it was only him and co-counsel were still there, therefore that's why he was removed completely. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That clears up my dilemma, especially as the Prosecution on several occasions and the Gotovina Defence said that in actual fact we cannot make any meritorious decisions, particularly when it comes to deciding upon agreed facts, so that does away with all the dilemmas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, at this point just by way of clarification, as we go through this, if counsel agrees to these facts, is it binding on the subsequent counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asking me a very difficult question. I think this is a question that you must ask -- you must resolve amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I just get just one particular clarification. I mean, is it -- I don't know the answer to that, if we agree on -- if we agree on a fact and Defence agrees on a fact, and another counsel comes in and says, "No, I don't agree on the fact," are we back to square one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You would be back to square one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, any other issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is clear now, because in the interests of the proceedings it wouldn't be a good idea if our position were revised when the new Defence team takes over, so we don't want to take over the competencies unless we're sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have anything to say as the last word?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That then brings us to the end of this conference. Court adjourns.
